article_title: Performance evaluation of large language models on Korean medical licensing examination: a three-year comparative analysis.
citation: Kim Hyun Jin, Jung Kiwook, Shin Sunghwan, Lee Wookeun, Lee Jun Hyung, Park Hee Sue, Choi Qute. (2025). Performance evaluation of large language models on Korean medical licensing examination: a three-year comparative analysis. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20066-x
title: KMLE 2022–2024 evaluation dataset of 942 Korean-language questions with physician-sourced images
description: A benchmark dataset of Korean Medical Licensing Examination questions from three consecutive years used to evaluate LLM medical knowledge in a non-English context. It contains "317 questions from 2022, 314 questions from 2023, and 311 questions from 2024, totaling 942 questions", spanning text-only and image-based A-type and R-type formats. Because the examination institute releases no official images, two licensed physicians independently sourced clinically relevant, de-identified images from open-access medical education resources; questions were preserved in their original Korean format and classified into seven medical specialties with an inter-annotator Cohen's kappa of 0.938.
requirements: Questions are sourced from publicly available KMLE materials released by the Korea Health Personnel Licensing Examination Institute (https://www.kuksiwon.or.kr)
constraints: Multimedia questions containing video or audio were excluded
Official images are not released by the institute, so images were physician-sourced rather than original exam images
target_learners: Medical school graduates and fourth-year students preparing for the Korean Medical Licensing Examination
target_learning_goals: Foundational medical knowledge and clinical skills assessed for medical licensure in Korea
examples: Automated API-based testing of GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro with zero temperature and a new session per problem
key_sources: Kim Hyun Jin, Jung Kiwook, Shin Sunghwan, Lee Wookeun, Lee Jun Hyung, Park Hee Sue, Choi Qute. (2025). Performance evaluation of large language models on Korean medical licensing examination: a three-year comparative analysis. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20066-x

article_title: Teaching differential diagnosis in primary care using an inverted classroom approach: student satisfaction and gain in skills and knowledge.
citation: Bösner S, Pickert J, Stibane T. (2015). Teaching differential diagnosis in primary care using an inverted classroom approach: student satisfaction and gain in skills and knowledge. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0346-x
title: K-Med-hosted inverted classroom seminar structure for differential diagnosis in primary care
description: The seminar is a 42-hour elective for fourth- and fifth-year medical students at an interactive skills lab, using "trained simulation patients and different models", closing with an OSCE. Each session follows a three-part structure: preparation via video and audio lectures on the web-based platform K-Med, face-to-face teaching with "simulation patients, training models, interactive small group work, and quiz exercises", and follow-up lectures with supplementary facultative reading. It is the only course at the faculty using the inverted classroom design.
requirements: Web-based learning platform hosting video and audio lectures for preparation and follow-up
Interactive skills lab with simulation patients, training models and small-group tutoring
constraints: Highly interactive small-group format limits enrolment to no more than 18 students
target_learners: fourth- and fifth-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: differential diagnosis of common primary care symptoms
clinical decision making under diagnostic uncertainty
examples: Modules use interdisciplinary clinical pictures from primary care routine, focusing on common aetiologies for lead symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnoea, abdominal pain, or vertigo/dizziness
key_sources: Bösner S, Pickert J, Stibane T. (2015). Teaching differential diagnosis in primary care using an inverted classroom approach: student satisfaction and gain in skills and knowledge. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0346-x
